messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina is a 30-year-old school counselor who had been proud of being the calm adult in the room, the person students sought out when they were frightened or overwhelmed. That sense of herself changed after an encounter with police nine months ago. She and her husband had been driving home from a friend’s birthday party when they were pulled over late at night. The officer approached the car already tense. Amina remembers the sharp smell of alcohol on his breath when he leaned toward her window, though she had not been drinking, and the crackle of his radio mixed with his raised voice. When her husband turned suddenly to reach for the registration in the glove compartment, the officer shouted and grabbed for his weapon. Amina froze. She can still recall how quickly ordinary movement became dangerous, how the officer’s abrupt gestures and yelling made the whole scene feel one second away from catastrophe. She believes she spoke at the wrong moment and moved too quickly when asked for her ID. Even now, what stays with her is the conviction that if she had acted differently, the stop would not have escalated the way it did.

In the weeks afterward, Amina tried to carry on at work, sitting with students in her office and walking noisy hallways between classes, but she no longer felt like the same person. She had come to believe there was something wrong with her, that other people could absorb a frightening experience and move on whereas she had somehow been ruined by it. She felt set apart even from her husband, who wanted to reassure her that they had survived and were safe. Because she blamed herself for how she had responded during the stop, she began shrinking away from anything that stirred strong feeling. If she sensed herself getting upset, she would abruptly change the subject, leave the room, or tell people she was tired. Invitations from friends were declined, not only because she did not want to talk about what happened, but because even the possibility of feeling happy or hopeful seemed risky, as if letting her guard down would expose how damaged she really was. She increasingly kept to herself, both at home and at school.

That withdrawal gradually altered the shape of her days. At work, she started eating lunch alone in her office with the door closed rather than in the staff room. She limited casual conversations with teachers and kept student meetings tightly structured so nothing emotional would spill beyond what she felt able to manage. After school, she often went straight home and avoided social visits entirely. Living that way made her world smaller and lonelier, and the loneliness fed what she already believed about herself: that she was no longer like other people, that she had become isolated in some fundamental way. The more she avoided situations that might bring warmth, closeness, or strong feeling, the more convincing it seemed that there really was something broken in her.

Her beliefs also kept her body in a state of readiness. Because she saw herself as someone who had failed in a dangerous moment, she was certain she could not trust herself to judge safety properly again. That conviction made her intensely watchful. In the school hallways, sudden movements by students—an arm thrown up in excitement, a teenager rushing past her doorway—put her immediately on guard. She scans entrances, notices who is moving quickly, and sits in meetings where she can see the door. Even at home on the couch beside her husband, she finds she cannot relax, though part of her knows she is in a safe place. When she catches herself monitoring everyone around her like this, it seems to confirm her harshest view of herself: normal people do not live braced for impact, she thinks, so there must be something deeply wrong with her.

That constant alarm has, in turn, made the world feel full of reminders. On days when she is exhausted, her control slips and she becomes especially vulnerable to being pulled back into the stop. Loud noises in the school building—the slam of a locker, a shouted voice in the corridor, the sudden burst of the PA system—make her heart jump before she can think. If she passes a parent at pickup who smells of alcohol, she feels a jolt of dread and has to fight the urge to leave. Because she has narrowed her life so much, she arrives at work already depleted, and in that worn-down state the triggers feel even closer to the surface. To protect herself she avoids assemblies, noisy common areas, celebratory staff events, and difficult conversations with colleagues or family; yet this constant retreat leaves her even more tense and watchful, as if danger is always just about to break through.

By the time Amina sought help, her husband had begun telling her that he missed her even when she was sitting next to him. At school, she was worried students were noticing how easily she startled and how often she cut meetings short. What finally brought her in was not one dramatic setback but the realization that she was living every day as though that traffic stop were still unfolding. She is frightened that if she keeps going this way, she will end up entirely cut off from other people and unable to do the work that once mattered most to her. At the same time, she is quietly hoping that treatment might help her feel less on guard, less ashamed, and less alone.
